records.our_prose: Flint corn is a warm-season crop here, sown once the soil reaches 60°F, roughly two weeks after the last spring frost. Season length is the binding constraint: favor an early flint and sow at the first warm soil. In the coldest zones a short-season flint like Painted Mountain (about 85 days, and tolerant of cold spring soil) is the dependable pick, where a full-season flint may not fully field-dry before frost and must finish drying under cover.

records.our_prose: Keep flint corn away from sweet corn and popcorn. Its pollen will drift in and spoil them, making sweet corn starchy and stopping popcorn from popping. Keep them at least 300 feet apart, or, since that is a lot of room, plant them so they tassel about two weeks apart instead.
records.source_context: As mentioned previously, because sweet corn is wind pollinated, quality is best if the stands are isolated from field corn, popcorn, and ornamental corn, as well as from other types of sweet corn. Isolation, in this sense, means either planting the crops at least 300 feet apart, or staggering plantings so that there is a 10 to 14 day difference in maturity between crops.

records.our_prose: A short-season, cold-hardy open-pollinated flint developed for northern and high-elevation gardens, with 6- to 7-inch ears of gold, orange, red, and purple kernels. It reaches dry grain in roughly 85 days and tolerates cold spring soil better than almost any other corn, so it is the reliable choice where the season is short. Grind it into cornmeal or flour.
